title: Parameter Symmetries Determine Representational Geometry in Overparameterized Nonlinear Networks
claim: Different parameterizations can yield identical functions with uncorrelated representations, and different functions can share correlated representations, so representation and function dissociate.
layout: 2 panels; A grid of neuron-symmetry cards, B 2x2 heatmap/RSM graph with ρ labels
description: Panel A is a grid of rounded, color-coded cards showing a reference neuron and the symmetry transformations that act on it. The left column holds Reference, Constant and Rescaling neurons. The next columns show Duplicates, Zero group, Linear duplicates, Linear group, Constant duplicates and Constant group. Each card draws small neuron icons with colored input and output weights and weight labels such as a_K, b*, w*, with a sum constraint (e.g. Σ a_d = a*) at the bottom. Panel B is a 2x2 arrangement of gray boxes. Each box holds stacked red-blue input-space heatmaps with decision boundaries and a green lower-triangular RSM. Boxes are linked by labeled connectors (ρ≈0 or ρ≈1), and a small XOR input-space diagram sits in the center. Green RSMs and red-blue heatmaps draw the eye first.
caption: Parameter symmetries can doubly dissociate function and representation. (A) Parameter symmetries let networks implement the same function via different parameterizations. They act on individual neurons (e.g., positive scaling for ReLU networks), redistribute or cancel computation across groups (duplicates, zero groups), or couple groups of neurons through algebraic structure in the activation σ (linear or constant duplicates, linear or constant groups). (B) Gradient descent from random initializations yields six distinct two-neuron ReLU networks solving XOR (center), shown as input-space heatmaps with neuron decision boundaries overlaid. They form two families (top left and bottom right) that solve the same task using different functions, with RSMs of solutions from opposite families being nearly uncorrelated. Crucially, such representational variability persists even when the function is held fixed: overparameterized networks implementing exactly the same function can have nearly uncorrelated RSMs (top and bottom). Conversely, networks implementing different functions can have highly correlated RSMs (left and right), yielding a double dissociation.
abstract: Representations are routinely used across machine learning, psychology, and neuroscience to draw inferences about the computations of biological and artificial systems. Such inferences presume that the geometry of these representations reflects the computation being performed. For artificial neural networks, however, the extent to which the function a network computes constrains this geometry remains unclear. One key obstacle is that these networks admit parameter symmetries: changes in parameterization that preserve function exactly while reshaping representational geometry. Here, we show that a broad class of parameter symmetries acts on representations through just three primitive feature transformations: addition, duplication, and scaling. This feature-level characterization yields a closed-form decomposition of representational geometry into essential and auxiliary components, revealing how representational degeneracy can exist without and grows with overparameterization even when function is held fixed. Finally, we establish conditions under which implementation-level selection rules resolve this degeneracy, yielding identifiable geometries in which features are weighted according to their contributions to the network's function. Together, our results delineate when representational geometry can support inferences about computation, and when it cannot.
